documentation.range: This species is endemic to the Solomon Island archipelago, including Bougainville and Buka (Papua New Guinea), and most forested islands in the Solomons including the Shortland group,  Choiseul, Vella lavella,  New Georgia, Tetepare,  Vangunu, Isabel, Guadalcanal,  Ngela, Malaita, Makira, Ugi, and Santa Ana islands (McCoy  2006).
documentation.population: There is no quantitative information on the population status of this skink, but McCoy (2006) states that "many populations of Corucia are now threatened by habitat destruction. Also, gross over-collecting of Corucia in the Solomons by animal dealers supplying the foreign pet trade, has necessitated its CITES Appendix II status". However, Hagen and Bull (2011) in their pioneering telemetry study of this species found that "all C. zebrata individuals that were followed spent considerable time in the tree canopies, where they have a low detection probability". Thus they conclude that "any survey to determine population levels in a particular habitat will be unreliable using current techniques" (Hagen and Bull 2011). I. Hagen (pers. comm. 2012) reports that C. zebrata were only encountered in sufficient numbers to conduct population genetic studies on one island in the archipelago, Ugi, where ten individuals were collected in two days (Hagen, unpubl. thesis); elsewhere the species was not recorded during longer searches (Tetepare), or was recorded as isolated individuals (Ngela); for the remaining Solomon Islands and the Papuan territories, no recent data is available (Hagen unpbl. thesis). Detection probabilities appear to be variable throughout the archipelago, making it difficult to compare abundances across islands (Hagen unpubl. thesis); however local perceptions appear to support evidence that species occurs at higher densities on Ugo Island than elsewhere (Hagen, unpubl. thesis). Although subpopulations throughout the archipelago are "clearly depleted" as a result of pressures from forest loss and harvesting (mainly for consumption) (I. Hagen pers. comm. 2012), no data is available on the timing or scale of declines. Forest habitat is severely fragmented within the Solomon Islands but this species can persist in secondary forest and, although absent from non-forested areas, it is not presently clear either whether existing forest patches are large enough to support viable subpopulations, or whether the intervening matrix represents a barrier to dispersal (I. Hagen pers. comm. 2012).
documentation.habitats: McCoy (2006) describes this nocturnal skink as 'sheltering by day in hollows or amongst dense foliage in the larger forest trees, the crevices in strangler fig trees Ficus spp. are a favourite habitat. It is almost completely arboreal......and... it is completely herbivorous...". Hagen and Bull (2011) found that "all C. zebrata individuals that we followed spent considerable time in the tree canopies". Hagen and Bull (2011) found most individuals within cavities of large tree trunks.
documentation.threats: This species is threatened by habitat loss resulting from logging and forest degradation, which is widespread throughout the Solomon Islands. Illegal collection for the pet trade is typically closely-linked to logging, and may be ongoing to some degree despite CITES controls although the scale is unknown (I. Hagen pers. comm. 2012). Harvesting for food by local human populations is likely to place additional pressure on this species.
documentation.measures: There are no known species-specific conservation measures in place for this species. It is not known if it is present in any protected areas. There is a need to control the illegal export of this species from the Solomon Islands. It is listed in Appendix II of CITES.
documentation.use_trade: Leary (1991) reviews the live reptile and amphibian export trade from the Solomon Islands for just two years; 1989 and 1990. Of the 27,675 reptiles and frogs officially exported in these two years, 7,469 or 27% were Solomon Island prehensile-tailed skink (Corucia zebrata). This legal trade has now ended, however, illegal export of Solomon Islands fauna continues, but probably a a much lower level then previously (M. McCoy, pers comm. 2012). Demand in Europe and the US may also have declined as a result of captive breeding (I. Hagen pers. comm. 2012). There is, however, no way of quantifying the current scale of illegal exports (I. Hagen pers. comm. 2012). This species has long been eaten by bush-dwelling people in the Solomons where it is considered a delicacy. In the past it was actively sought and collected, although nowadays, while it is still eaten, its collection would appear to be on a much reduced level as readily available imported processed foods (tinned fish and meat) have replaced it as a source of protein (M. McCoy pers. comm. November 2011). The species is nonetheless still commonly consumed across the archipelago, although hunting has recently declined in the Western Province and in at least the less remote areas of Choiseul and Isabel (I. Hagen pers. comm. 2012).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Near Threatened because this species is probably in significant decline (but probably at a rate of less than 30% over ten years) because of widespread habitat loss through much of its range, and illegal overcollection for the pet trade. The population is thought to be severely fragmented, and while a continuing decline is underway in the extent and quality of its habitat and the number of mature individuals the extent of occurrence is greater than 100,000 km2 and its area of occupancy cannot be calculated with certainty.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: A unique and specialised species, in a monotypic genus, described by Gray (1855). Köhler (1997) referred the Bougainville and Buka populations to the subspecies Corucia zebrata alfredschmidti based on the colour and pattern of live animals. McCoy (2006), on the basis of this description, suggests that this would also include the Shortland Islands populations. All individuals to the east of the Shortland Islands are thus referred to as Corucia zebrata zebrata.
